items.title: OpenAI's upcoming chat-and-work merger in ChatGPT signals the end of all-you-can-prompt pricing
items.content:
OpenAI combines the Chat and Work modes into a single interface. Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans will share a common, token-based quota for ChatGPT and Codex. More complex models consume more of this quota, while simple instant chats do not count toward it. In practice, this is likely to result in a decline in ChatGPT’s quality for heavy users on lower-cost plans.

items.title: Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds
items.content:
A study by Vals AI tested 25 AI models for alignment with Chinese government positions and found surprising results. Chinese models respond to political questions less uniformly than expected, and Western models occasionally adopt official Beijing positions too. The language of the prompt had an especially strong effect on the political slant of responses.
The article Chinese AI models are politically complex, not just government mouthpieces, study finds appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent
items.content:
The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System.



TL;DaR




What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to.



Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+.



Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent.



Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster).



Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured.




What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent?



It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person.



The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure.



Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent?



DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng, a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking.



How does the Router-Worker architecture work?



The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work.



In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model:




Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events.



Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work.



Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed.



Subscription: later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention.




The main session runs the dsh-superagent-router preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs dsh-superagent-worker. Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the execution doc.



Proactive work is gated. The authorization doc defines 3 accept modes: off, observe (default) and auto. In observe, the agent only records what it would have accepted.



The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop. 






&&








How does it perform?



DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per ifeng’s account of the report.




Super-agent: p50 of 12.4 minutes, p95 of 15.7 minutes.



Single session plus subagents, neutral prompt: p95 of 29.5 minutes. No p50 was given.



Why: under the neutral prompt, the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs.



Router load: as arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8. Per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds.




An ablation removed direct event pass-through. Router decisions rose about 30%, and cache-read tokens rose about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M. All figures are self-reported and come from secondary reports of the report.



How does dsh-superagent compare with other GitHub coding agents?



FeatureDeepSeek dsh-superagentGitHub Copilot cloud agentClaude Code ActionOpenAI CodexTriggerMention by allowed person; written rulesIssue assignment, chat, API, Slack and more@claude mention, issue assignment, workflow prompt@Codex in Slack; cloud tasksUnasked (proactive) workYes, rule-gated; observe by defaultYes, via automationsYes, via workflow eventsNot disclosedParallel isolated sessionsYes, 1 per TicketNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedWhere it runsYour machine (Harness profile)GitHub, in the backgroundYour GitHub Actions runnerCodex cloudChat sourceFeishu (optional)Slack, TeamsNot disclosedSlackLicenseMITNot disclosedMITCLI agent open sourceAvailabilityResearch prototypeAll paid Copilot plansYour API key or cloud providerChatGPT Plus and above



Key Takeaways




DeepSeek released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed proactive coding agent prototype.



A Router dispatches work; isolated Worker sessions execute each Ticket.



Simulated p95 task time: 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for a single session.



Proactive work stays in observe mode until a team switches it on.



It runs with full OS-user access, so isolate it before use.
















Check out the GitHub repo, the setup guide and the design docs. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners
items.content:
Researchers in Luxembourg put ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini on the therapist's couch and found a safety problem: a warm, empathetic conversational style is enough to make the models tell coherent stories of suffering about their own training, with scores in the moderate-to-severe range on clinical anxiety scales. This could put mentally vulnerable users at risk. Anthropic's Claude, the model its makers anthropomorphize the most, was the only one that consistently refused to play along.
The article Empathetic prompts can turn AI chatbots into seemingly traumatized conversational partners appeared first on The Decoder.
items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.summary: Researchers in Luxembourg found that warm, empathetic prompting led ChatGPT, Grok, and Gemini to invent coherent stories of suffering about their own training, scoring in the moderate-to-severe range on clinical anxiety scales, a potential risk for mentally vulnerable users. Anthropic's Claude was the only tested model that consistently refused to play along.
items.reasoning: A notable independent safety finding about model behavior under persona-style empathetic prompting, with direct user-wellbeing implications and a striking behavioral divergence between frontier labs' models. Research-level rather than release-level significance.

items.title: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon
items.content:
Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights. Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF, an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama. For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine.



TL;DR




Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question.



Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama.



Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported).



Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac.




What is Drex Max?



Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated.



Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks.



How does Drex Max work?



The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence.



Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window.




&&&







How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks?



All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI,




Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96.



Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4.



Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows.



Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18.



JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071).




The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong.



How do you run Drex Max locally?



Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API.



RuntimeHardwareCheckpointImagesPythonNVIDIA GPUbf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB)Yesllama.cpp forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB)NoOllama forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUFNoKapitsa v0.2.25+Apple SiliconQ8_0 GGUF or affine Q4NoMLXApple Siliconaffine Q4 (14.45 GB)No



The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa.



Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile.



Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips.



Drex Max vs other decision models



Drex Max v1Drex v2.0Drex v1.5Jev 1.13.0Parameters27B dense35B MoE, ~3B active9BNot publishedMax context262,144131,072131,072Not disclosedInputsText, JSON, imagesText (vision tower dropped)TextNot disclosedWeightsOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MClosed, hostedSmallest local fileAffine Q4, 24 GB+ MacQ8_0, 36.9 GBQ8_0, ~9.5 GBNot applicablePublic Decision Index67.52 (v0.4)61.25 (v0.3.1)58.08 (v0.3.1)57.96JevBench92.2%85.7%Not disclosed86.6%AA Decision Index6458Not listed58Hosted price$0.03 / 1K decisions (launch)$0.06 / 1K decisions$0.04 / 1K decisions$42 / 1M tasks



Nace AI team states that Decision Index 0.4 uses the same public suite as 0.3.1. 



Key Takeaways




Drex Max v1 weights are now public under Nace.AI Open RAIL-M.



It scores 67.52 on Decision Index 0.4, above Drex v2.0 (61.25).



A 4-bit build runs on 24 GB Apple Silicon Macs via Kapitsa or MLX.



Q8_0 on an M5 Pro matched H100 bf16 within 0.02.



Local Mac and CPU paths are text only for now.




Check out the model weights, Q8_0 GGUF, code and docs, Tweet and cloud console. 











Thanks to the Nace AI team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by Nace AI.

items.content_html:
Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights. Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF, an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama. For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine.

TL;DR

Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question.

Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama.

Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported).

Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac.

What is Drex Max?

Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated.

Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks.

How does Drex Max work?

The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence.

Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window.

&&&

How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks?

All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI,

Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96.

Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4.

Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows.

Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18.

JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071).

The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong.

How do you run Drex Max locally?

Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API.

RuntimeHardwareCheckpointImagesPythonNVIDIA GPUbf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB)Yesllama.cpp forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB)NoOllama forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUFNoKapitsa v0.2.25+Apple SiliconQ8_0 GGUF or affine Q4NoMLXApple Siliconaffine Q4 (14.45 GB)No

The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa.

Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile.

Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips.

Drex Max vs other decision models

Drex Max v1Drex v2.0Drex v1.5Jev 1.13.0Parameters27B dense35B MoE, ~3B active9BNot publishedMax context262,144131,072131,072Not disclosedInputsText, JSON, imagesText (vision tower dropped)TextNot disclosedWeightsOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MOpen, Nace.AI Open RAIL-MClosed, hostedSmallest local fileAffine Q4, 24 GB+ MacQ8_0, 36.9 GBQ8_0, ~9.5 GBNot applicablePublic Decision Index67.52 (v0.4)61.25 (v0.3.1)58.08 (v0.3.1)57.96JevBench92.2%85.7%Not disclosed86.6%AA Decision Index6458Not listed58Hosted price$0.03 / 1K decisions (launch)$0.06 / 1K decisions$0.04 / 1K decisions$42 / 1M tasks

Nace AI team states that Decision Index 0.4 uses the same public suite as 0.3.1. 

Key Takeaways

Drex Max v1 weights are now public under Nace.AI Open RAIL-M.

It scores 67.52 on Decision Index 0.4, above Drex v2.0 (61.25).

A 4-bit build runs on 24 GB Apple Silicon Macs via Kapitsa or MLX.

Q8_0 on an M5 Pro matched H100 bf16 within 0.02.

Local Mac and CPU paths are text only for now.

Check out the model weights, Q8_0 GGUF, code and docs, Tweet and cloud console.

Thanks to the Nace AI team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by Nace AI.

items.title: Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would
items.content:
Adobe Research and UC San Diego built EditAgent, an AI system that edits images more like a Photoshop pro. Instead of retrying the same general-purpose editor over and over, the agent picks the right specialized tool for each task and lets a standard language model choose the best result based on measured image data. The approach works, but it needs about ten times the compute.
The article Adobe is testing how well AI agents can use editing tools like a Photoshop professional would appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: Google wants video AI to understand what people need as they work
items.content:
A Google-led research team built StreamVibe, a video agent designed to watch people cook or assemble furniture and speak up only when help is needed. A benchmark shows that none of the tested models reliably pick the right moment in longer videos, as errors compound and response quality drops sharply.
The article Google wants video AI to understand what people need as they work appeared first on The Decoder.

items.title: OpenAI is steering ChatGPT users toward more paid usage
items.content:
OpenAI is now capping the number of paid ChatGPT accounts per device and payment card. Users who hit the limit can't start new subscriptions, and affected accounts can't be used on that device. Logging out doesn't automatically free up a spot. The policy will likely hit users who've been juggling multiple cheap subscriptions to maximize usage, pushing them toward pricier options like buying extra credits.
The article OpenAI is steering ChatGPT users toward more paid usage appeared first on The Decoder.
items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.summary: OpenAI is capping the number of paid ChatGPT accounts per device and payment card, blocking new subscriptions at the limit and preventing affected accounts from being used on that device, even after logout. The policy pushes users juggling multiple cheap subscriptions toward pricier options like extra credits.
items.reasoning: A monetization and access-policy change at the leading AI consumer product, notable as part of the broader shift from flat-rate toward usage-based pricing, but routine business news without capability implications.

items.content: Outsourcing planning to AI can lead people to surrender their own critical thinking, which can have potentially deadly results in places like the backcountry.
items.author: Christine Peterson
items.summary: Wired reports on hikers who outsourced backcountry trip planning to chatbots with potentially dangerous results, highlighting how relying on AI for route and safety planning can erode critical thinking. The piece frames chatbot errors in wilderness contexts as a concrete physical-risk problem, not just an accuracy nuisance.
items.reasoning: A real and newsworthy angle on AI overreliance with physical safety stakes, but it is journalism about known chatbot limitations rather than a model, policy, or capability development. Modest frontier relevance.

items.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
items.content: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza StricklandAs features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”
